source.title: Temperature Balancing, Layer-wise Weight Analysis, and Neural Network Training
source.authors: Ye-Fan Zhou; Tian-Yu Pang; Keqin Liu; Charles H. Martin; Michael W. Mahoney; Yao-Qing Yang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text including appendices is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own experiments on layer-wise weight-spectrum metrics and their association with test accuracy, and applies those metrics during training. These results bear on V7's measured-properties version, using PL Alpha Hill and test accuracy rather than magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or an explicit train-test gap.
record.gate_note: The main TempBalance versus optimizer and scheduler comparisons are new method performance comparisons, not by themselves results on the claim's versions. The relevant claim-bearing results are weight-spectrum measurements and the reported relationship between PL Alpha Hill distributions and test accuracy. Cited findings about generalization measures and other studies are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares adaptive optimizers with momentum SGD on CIFAR100 under limited tuning, bearing on V4. The reader incorrectly excludes these comparisons. Its spectral measurements do not test V7: PL exponents are different from magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, and test accuracy is different from the train-test gap.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase accurately describes the authors' conclusion: TempBalance balances layer-wise spectral diagnostics and improves test performance, and they associate PL Alpha Hill with model quality. They do not test V7. They additionally report that the tested Adam-based methods do not outperform the SGD baseline.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses PL Alpha Hill weight-spectrum measurements to assign layer-wise learning rates during training; it does not perturb weights by magnitude-scaled amounts or measure the train-test gap described in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differences across architecture and dataset groups in the layer-wise distributions; TempBalance changes learning-rate assignments relative to CAL. It also reports that postponing TempBalance to epochs 2, 5, or 10 does not affect test performance, but that result concerns training performance rather than V7's sharpness-gap measure.

fits_no_version.finding: TempBalance concentrates layer-wise PL Alpha Hill distributions nearer 2 relative to CAL.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Assigning learning rates using layer-wise spectral exponents changes the distribution of those exponents.

fits_no_version.finding: Output-covariance and Hessian spectral exponents correlate across six checkpoints of a spectrally regularized MLP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Power-law spectral exponents of these two matrices can covary during training with spectral regularization.

record.problems: The reported spectral-distribution relationship is qualitative in the supplied text and does not measure train-test gaps. The covariance-Hessian correlation has no reported coefficient or uncertainty in the text. Several related plots do not provide numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row cap. The paper's test-accuracy comparisons for CAL, TempBalance, SNR, and other optimizers are excluded from claim-version rows because they compare the paper's proposed training method and do not measure a behavior named in V1–V8. The paper's reported test-accuracy improvements and optimizer comparisons appear in Sections 4.2–4.3, Figures 3–8 and 17, and Appendix G, Table 7.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out performance.
Continued improvement beyond the width needed for zero training error. Width experiments report test accuracy without establishing interpolation or training to convergence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Training-performance comparisons, broader tuning, switching optimizers, and adaptive-versus-SGD comparisons on language models. Table 7 compares schedulers using Adam, not Adam against SGD.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
All: magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, train-test gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

missing.what: Restore the incorrectly excluded V4 comparisons: Adam and LAMB versus momentum SGD with cosine annealing on ResNet18/34 and CIFAR100. Appendix E reports that adaptive methods do not outperform SGD, with learning-rate searches and fixed weight decay and momentum parameters. Extract each optimizer's accuracy and uncertainty from Figure 17; Table 2 supplies SGD baselines of 78.31 ± 0.05% and 78.98 ± 0.14%. The supplied figure text does not reveal adaptive accuracies, and the authors' statement alone cannot distinguish equal from worse performance.
missing.locator: Section 4.2; Appendix E; Figure 17; Appendix D, Table 2

record.verdict_notes: No V4 verdict is assigned because the readable text establishes only that adaptive methods are no better than SGD, without distinguishing equality from worse performance. The V4 comparisons were declared omitted, but their stated exclusion rationale is incorrect and requires correction. None of the existing rows supports a verdict on any version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Test error across widths beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparisons.

Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance and explicit train-test generalization gaps; comparisons against norm- and margin-based generalization measures; CIFAR-10 and SVHN without augmentation as specified by the version.
Removing memorized examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-wise PL Alpha Hill distributions after TempBalance and CAL training.
rows.measure: Distribution of layer-wise PL Alpha Hill values; paper reports TB gives a more concentrated distribution, with mean and median approaching 2.
rows.baseline: CAL; exact distribution values not stated in text.
rows.value: TB; exact distribution values not stated in text.
rows.note: Paper reports grouped distributions, not exact per-model distribution statistics in the supplied text.
rows.check: The reported spectral concentration is supported, but it measures neither magnitude-aware sharpness nor its association with generalization gaps. It describes the proposed method's effect on its own diagnostic.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Measured PL exponents for output covariance and Hessian and compared their association.
rows.measure: Correlation between fitted PL exponents; authors describe a strong correlation.
rows.value: strong correlation; numerical coefficient not stated
rows.note: This is a relationship between spectra of two matrices, not magnitude-aware sharpness tracking an explicit generalization gap; retained only as a related measurement.
rows.check: Wrong subject: Figure 9 uses a one-hidden-layer MLP with 2000 neurons, not ResNet18. Spectral regularization deliberately induces a power-law output-covariance spectrum. The correlation with Hessian exponents measures no claim version.
